summary.en: Venezuelan authorities detained former world champion boxer Linares while appointing a gay foreign minister, reflecting internal political shifts, and workers staged a 24‑hour strike at Miraflores Palace as the government allocated US$12 billion of oil revenue to support the bolívar. A special-forces soldier who wagered $400,000 on Maduro's removal appeared in court, and a marine died after falling overboard during the first US military operation in the Caribbean. Trump announced Venezuela as a new acquisition and claimed superior armaments, while a Venezuelan military attaché resumed work in Minsk and EU asset freezes targeted Haitian gangs linked to the crisis. Two battle-related deaths occurred in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: Venezuelanske myndigheter arresterte den tidligere verdensmesteren i boksing Linares mens de utnevnte en homofil utenriksminister, noe som gjenspeiler interne politiske skift, og arbeidere holdt en 24‑timmers streik ved Miraflores-palasset da regjeringen avsatte US$12 milliarder av oljeinntektene til å støtte bolívaren. En spesialstyrkesoldat som hadde satset $400 000 på Maduros avsettelse, dukket opp i retten, og en marine døde etter å ha falt overbord under den første amerikanske militæroperasjonen i Karibia. Trump kunngjorde Venezuela som et nytt anskaffelse og hevdet overlegen beväpning, mens en venezuelansk militærattaché gjenopptok arbeidet i Minsk og EU-frysing av eiendeler målrettet haitiske gjenger knyttet til krisen. To dødsfall i kamp ble registrert i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro as well as Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
